![What is a Biological Signature?](./cover.png)

A fingerprint identifies you from a patch of skin the size of a stamp. That is
the trick: a few well-chosen features stand in for the whole person, and you
never need the person.

A biological fingerprint does the same with molecules. A handful of genes,
proteins, or metabolites — the small molecules a body makes as it burns fuel and
builds tissue — carry a pattern, and the pattern is enough to tell one condition
from another. This tumour and not that one. Infected, not healthy. When that
pattern is measured rather than eyeballed, we call it a **signature**.

## Finding one is feature selection

One lab test reads tens of thousands of genes at once; patients are slow and
costly to enrol. A gene chip, or microarray, hands you 20,000 readings on 70
people, nearly all of them noise for your question, and a model given all 20,000
will fit that noise perfectly. The signature is the short list you keep.

1. **Measure wide.** Every feature on every sample.
2. **Find the groups.** If you already know who belongs to which group, you
   have what the next two steps need. If you don't, let a clustering method
   propose the groups first.
3. **Select.** Score each feature by how well it separates the groups. A
   *t*-test asks how far apart it puts the two group averages, relative to how
   much it wanders within each group. Mutual information asks a different
   question — how much does knowing this feature tell you about which group a
   sample is in — and so it can catch separations a difference of averages
   misses. Or let a model that is charged a price for every feature it uses
   (lasso, elastic net) drop the rest for you.
4. **Validate on data you never touched.** Hold part of the data back, fit on
   the rest, test on the part you held back, and rotate — that is
   cross-validation, and each turn is a fold. Redo the selection inside every
   fold.

Skip step 4 and the number you report is too good. Choose the genes using all
your samples and the ones you held back are no longer fresh: those genes were
chosen *because* they split those exact samples.
[Ambroise and McLachlan (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.102102699) showed
this bias drags the reported cross-validation error towards zero, and that
redoing selection inside each fold pushes it back up.

## Golub's fifty genes are the canonical case

Dodging that trap is what made the founding example credible. Two kinds of acute
leukemia, ALL and AML, look alike down a microscope but take opposite
chemotherapies, and the call rested on four separate specialist lab tests —
good, yet errors happened. [Golub and colleagues
(1999)](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.286.5439.531) measured 6,817 genes in 38
samples from acute leukemia patients. Clustering, told nothing about who had
which disease, nearly found the split on its own: it sorted the patients into
two groups, one holding 24 ALL patients and a single AML, the other holding 10
AML patients and 3 ALL. They then trained a 50-gene predictor and tested it on
34 fresh samples from other leukemia banks. Fifty features out of
6,817: a signature.

The same four steps run on other data. Animals shed DNA into water, and a few
marker sequences in a river sample say a jaguar was there. Read from starlight,
an exoplanet's atmosphere can show gases that chemistry alone would struggle to
produce.

**Further reading:** [Guyon and Elisseeff
(2003)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/guyon03a.html) on feature selection;
[Meinshausen and Bühlmann
(2010)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2010.00740.x) on keeping only
features that survive resampling.
